## Design

### 2026-10-06 — October 6th- Used KiCad to design the schematic (first time using KiCad)

**2.75h**

October 6th- Used KiCad to design the schematic (first time using KiCad)

I learnt how to use KiCad!
I decided to use the ESP32-Wroom as the microcontroller for this project as I have used ESP32s before but I was not expecting to almost run out of GPIOs (more on that later). I started by connecting the ten buttons (nine on the encryption side and one on the decryption side) to the ESP32. I then connected two single pole triple throw switches, one for switching between encryption and decryption and one to control substitution cypher mode. Then I realised that I forgot to put resistors in the button circuits and went back to do that.

![Screenshot 2026-10-06 184144](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/ffemyHmiOqHaF7D7CD5FnDqX9mm68g95/4c8789b94f31bdb5c51157a8e46d69bcc03edfb03781d7968b5b62ebf7703fa2.png)
At that point, I started to think about how I would display the decrypted letters. My first idea was to use a 16 segment LED display, but that took up (to no-one's surprise) 16 GPIOs which was more than I had available. I then looked at LED matrix displays, which could take up fewer pins as it uses SPI, but would be harder to attach to a PCB.  After looking at the pros and cons, I chose to keep trying to use the 16 segment LED display after realising you could wire multiple segments to one GPIO,  which would use less pins.

 I then spent some time figuring out which segments are only used at the same time as another when displaying the alphabet so I could wire them together without affecting other letters and finding other ways to display each letter so that it doesn't get affected by the segments being wired together.

![display sheet](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/ffemyHmiOqHaF7D7CD5FnDqX9mm68g95/9fa7ce5d9500eb547dd0fb8344cb339004cd4bb590ffc7b8b4ea4661aa5fe51e.jpg)

I was eventually able to reduce the pin count from 16 to 10 which was still one too many GPIOs. To free up a  GPIO, I replaced the triple throw switch for switching between encryption and decryption with a double throw switch so the LED display could be connected.

However, since there isn't a symbol for a 16 segment LED display in KiCad I had to use KiCad's Symbol Editor to design a custom symbol for the LED display.

![Screenshot 2026-10-06 222655](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/ffemyHmiOqHaF7D7CD5FnDqX9mm68g95/07b0a2b84e452b5297522fc9c36a9ab2c19988bfb82d5ff4848410fb1c34f0b8.png)

After that, all there was left to do was add the LED to the schematic and connect it to the ESP32!

![Screenshot 2026-10-06 224222](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/ffemyHmiOqHaF7D7CD5FnDqX9mm68g95/667b486355b3fbd06e673a6c70722417864476f26340ed5e0aa22cd5088fadd8.png)

Have a nice day!
